warmup.q: MoveMate's master list of every @Inventory class is written with Dependencies(aggregating = false, *filesOfEveryListedClass). You add a new file, Mirror.kt, with one more @Inventory class, and build again without cleaning. What does the new master list contain?
options: The old classes without Mirror, until a clean build
Nothing: KSP stops with an error about the new file
warmup.why: KSP reprocesses the changed files and every file tied to an output that changed. A new file is tied to nothing yet, so the processor sees one class and writes a list of one over the old list, and the build stays green. The first option is what aggregating = true gives you. Section 3 runs both.

opening:
Picture the family a week after the move. They repack one box: the reading lamp gets a second bulb. The lamp's card has to change, and so does the master list on the fridge, the one sheet that names every box in the house. Nobody wants to rewrite every card in the house for one bulb.

A build that redoes only what changed is fast, and KSP works that way out of the box. The catch is that it trusts you to say where each card came from. In lesson 2 you wrote Dependencies(false, file), with a promise that lesson 7 would explain it. Here it is: get that one argument wrong for the master list, and a later build hands you a list that has lost most of the house, with no error and a green build.

In this lesson, we'll watch KSP decide what to redo, write the master list as the right kind of output, break it twice on purpose, and hand the processor a job sheet of options. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started a week after the move, with one more bulb for the reading lamp. KSP redid the lamp's card and the master list, and read the other boxes again only because the list came from them. Then we broke the list twice, into a move with one mirror and into no list at all, and both builds stayed green.

In your own processors, find every Dependencies( and writeTo(, and ask of each output: does it list one box or many? If many, it says aggregating = true.

Next, we'll test a processor the way a library author does. How do you prove, in a test that runs in a second, that a generated builder accepts a lamp with no shade?

sections.h: Repacking one box: which files KSP reads again after an edit
sections.html:
A build turns your source files into a program you can run, and on a real project it runs dozens of times a day. Most of those runs follow a small edit. An incremental build redoes only the work that edit can affect and reuses the rest from the last run.

Gradle does this one task at a time. A task's inputs are the files and settings it reads. Before running a task, Gradle compares them with the last run, and if nothing changed, it skips the task and marks it UP-TO-DATE. It compares contents, not dates: touch Lamp.kt changes the file's time, and the KSP task stays UP-TO-DATE. Touching a file fools nobody.

KSP goes one level further, inside its own task. When a source file did change, KSP works out which files must be processed again. Those are the dirty files, and the processors see only them in round 1. Every output of a clean file comes back from a copy KSP keeps under build/kspCaches/.

Let's watch it decide. The playground gives each lesson its own source set, a group of source folders that Gradle compiles together. Lesson 7's, labs/ksp/app/src/l07, holds the four MoveMate classes, one per file, each with @Inventory, plus MovingDay.kt, which prints the cards, and its Java twin. The lesson's processor writes two kinds of output: a card per class, as in lesson 2, and one master list of every class, which we'll meet in the next section. The Gradle property ksp.incremental.log makes KSP write what it decided into labs/ksp/app/build/kspCaches/l07/logs/. After a first build, we added one comment line to Lamp.kt and built again:

./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true

kspDirtySet.log then read like this (empty sections trimmed):

Modified
  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt
Dirty:
  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Bookshelf.kt
  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt
  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Plant.kt
  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Box.kt

Dirty / All: 66.67%

One file was modified, and four were read again. MovingDay.kt and the Java file were not. That's the first thing to notice: KSP doesn't reprocess everything, and it doesn't reprocess only the edited file either. It follows the outputs back to their sources.

The card is the easy half. Lamp's card was written with these Dependencies:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a javac processor writing one card per class
JavaFileObject card = processingEnv.getFiler()
        .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name + "InventoryCard", cls);   // cls: the one element it came from
// META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors:  workbench.ksp.l07.CardProcessor,isolating
Kotlin
// lesson 2's card, written with KotlinPoet: it came from this class's own file, and nothing else
inventoryCardFile(cls).writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = false, cls.containingFile!!))

Read the Kotlin line aloud: "this card came from this class's file, and from nothing else." KSP calls that an isolating output: it depends only on the source files you name. Java has had annotation processors, programs that javac runs while it compiles, since Java 6, and KSP is Kotlin's own way to do that job for Kotlin code, without going through Java. The Java side has the same idea one level up. Gradle sorts whole javac processors into categories, and an isolating one must give exactly one originating element, the element the file came from, for each file it writes.

In the moving-house picture, Lamp.kt is the repacked box, and its card is the only card that must be redone because of it. The cards of the untouched boxes come back from storage. The picture breaks in one place: a real helper sees which box was repacked. KSP sees only what your Dependencies say, plus the types your processor looked up. It doesn't open boxes to check.

So why were Box, Bookshelf and Plant read again for one bulb? Because of the master list.

try.title: Edit one box and read what KSP read again
steps: From labs/, build lesson 7's source set once: ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true. Keep that flag on every command in this lesson. Gradle counts it as part of the task's setup, so a run without it makes the next run start over.
Run touch ksp/app/src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt, then the same build. Predict the status of kspL07Kotlin before you look.
Add a comment line at the end of Lamp.kt and build again. Open labs/ksp/app/build/kspCaches/l07/logs/kspDirtySet.log. Which files are under Dirty:, and which aren't?
Run the program with the command below, or its Java twin. Then remove your comment.

code.title: MovingDay.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.app.l07 // Prints the master list and one card per thing, through code KSP generated in this build: // MovingDayList (aggregating) and the inventoryCard() functions (isolating). // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayKt // ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true then read build/kspCaches/l07/logs/ fun main() { val things = listOf( Box("books", "study", 12_000), Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null), Bookshelf(3, listOf("Dune", "Emma")), Plant("fern", 2.5), ) println("MovingDayList: ${MovingDayList.names}") for (thing in things) println(MovingDayList.cardFor(thing)) }

alt.html: package workbench.ksp.app.l07; import java.util.List; // The Java twin of MovingDay.kt: Java calling the master list KSP generated in Kotlin. MovingDayList is a Kotlin // object, so Java reaches it through its INSTANCE field; the names property is the getter getNames(). // ./gradlew :ksp:app:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayJava public class MovingDayJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<Object> things = List.of( new Box("books", "study", 12_000, false), new Lamp("desk lamp", 1, null), new Bookshelf(3, List.of("Dune", "Emma")), new Plant("fern", 2.5, 7)); System.out.println("MovingDayList: " + MovingDayList.INSTANCE.getNames()); for (Object thing : things) System.out.println(MovingDayList.INSTANCE.cardFor(thing)); } }

After the comment, Modified lists only Lamp.kt, and Dirty: lists the four files with an @Inventory class (Dirty / All: 66.67% on our run), but not MovingDay.kt or MovingDayJava.java. The program prints MovingDayList: [Bookshelf, Box, Lamp, Plant] and one card per thing, such as Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null.

sections.h: The master list: an aggregating output that every box feeds
sections.html:
The master list is one file, MovingDayList.kt, that names every @Inventory class and hands out the right card for any of them:

public object MovingDayList {
  public val names: List<String> = listOf("Bookshelf", "Box", "Lamp", "Plant")

  public fun cardFor(thing: Any): String = when (thing) {
    is Bookshelf -> thing.inventoryCard()
    is Box -> thing.inventoryCard()
    is Lamp -> thing.inventoryCard()
    is Plant -> thing.inventoryCard()
    else -> error("MovingDayList has no card for ${thing::class.simpleName}")
  }
}

That's generated code, shown as KotlinPoet printed it. A list like this can't belong to one box. Change any class on it, and the list may change. Add a new class anywhere in the source set, and the list must change, though no file on the list was touched. KSP's docs call such an output aggregating: it "can be affected by changes in any source file". The opposite, isolating, depends "only on their specified sources".

Here is how the processor says so, and what the Java side writes:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: one file made from many classes
JavaFileObject list = processingEnv.getFiler()
        .createSourceFile(pkg + ".MovingDayList", classes.toArray(new Element[0]));
// Gradle can only mark the whole processor, in META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors:
//   workbench.ksp.l07.MasterListProcessor,aggregating
Kotlin
fun listDependencies(classes: List<KSClassDeclaration>): Dependencies =
    Dependencies(aggregating = true, *classes.mapNotNull { it.containingFile }.distinct().toTypedArray())

masterListFile(classes, listOptions).writeTo(codeGenerator, listDependencies(classes))

Read listDependencies aloud: "this list came from the file of every class on it, each file once, and new files can change it too." aggregating = true is the second half of that sentence. The two languages split the work differently. Gradle puts its category on a whole javac processor, and its isolating processors need exactly one originating element per file. KSP puts the category on each output, and an isolating output may name several files. If you build files with KotlinPoet, addOriginatingKSFile(file) on the top-level TypeSpec and writeTo(codeGenerator, aggregating = true) do the same job. KotlinPoet collects originating files only from top-level members, though, not from nested types.

The second log, kspSourceToOutputs.log, shows what KSP recorded. Each annotated file maps to its card and to the list, and one more key stands alone:

  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt:
    build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/LampInventoryCard.kt
    build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDayList.kt
  <AnyChanges is a virtual file; DO NOT USE.>:
    build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDayList.kt

That virtual key is how "any change" reaches the list: every edit dirties it, and a dirty list makes every file it came from dirty. KSP's label, DO NOT USE, is fair, because you never name the key yourself; aggregating = true does it for you. That explains the 66.67%: one edit, the whole list, and with it all four of its boxes.

Now add a fifth box. We created Rug.kt with @Inventory data class Rug(val size: String) and built again. The dirty set held all five annotated files (71.43%), and the program printed MovingDayList: [Bookshelf, Box, Lamp, Plant, Rug]. In the picture, the master list on the fridge is rewritten after any change to the house, from every box on it. The picture breaks here: a family would add one line for the rug. KSP rewrites the whole list, from scratch, from every file it came from.

An output that lists many boxes depends on all of them, and on boxes not packed yet. Mark it aggregating.

The price is visible in the log: every edit re-reads every box on the list. Still, MovingDay.kt stayed clean, and on a real project the cards of classes outside the list stay clean too. That's the right Dependencies. Let's see the wrong ones.

sections.h: Wrong Dependencies on purpose: a list that shrinks, and a list that vanishes
sections.html:
A wrong Dependencies doesn't fail the build. It fails a later build, after an ordinary edit, and only sometimes. So let's make the mistakes on purpose and watch. The lab's processor has a teaching switch that no real processor has: the option movemate.listDependencies in labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties replaces your Dependencies for the list with one of three wrong ones.

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: what Gradle does with a javac processor's originating elements
filer.createSourceFile(pkg + ".MovingDayList");          // isolating processor, no element:
                                                          // Gradle recompiles every source file (slow, safe)
filer.createSourceFile(pkg + ".MovingDayList", lamp);    // isolating, one element: Gradle trusts it
Kotlin
// Naive: three Dependencies for the master list, each wrong in its own way
Dependencies(false, *files)      // isolating: right after an edit, wrong after a new box
Dependencies(false)              // no file at all: the list belongs to nobody
Dependencies.ALL_FILES           // safe, but every edit dirties every file

The first one deserves a word of credit. Dependencies(false, *files) names every file the list came from, so an edit to an existing box still redoes it: a dirty list makes all its files dirty, whatever its category. Its flaw is the new box. We set the switch to isolating and built once. A changed option is a changed input, so that build ran KSP over every file (Dirty / All: 100.00%), and the list's AnyChanges key was gone. Then we added Mirror.kt with one more @Inventory class:

Modified
  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Mirror.kt
Dirty:
  src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Mirror.kt

Dirty / All: 12.50%

A new file is tied to no output yet, so nothing marked the list as dirty. The processor saw one class and wrote a list of one, right over the old one. The build passed. Then the program ran:

MovingDayList: [Mirror]
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: MovingDayList has no card for Box
	at workbench.ksp.app.l07.MovingDayList.cardFor(MovingDayList.kt:13)

A move with one mirror in it. That's the warm-up's answer: only Mirror.

The second one is lesson 2's promise, paid. With Dependencies(false) and no file, the list belongs to no box. We switched to none, built once, and added one comment to MovingDay.kt, a file with no annotation at all. Only MovingDay.kt was dirty (12.50%), the processor found no @Inventory class to list, and KSP filed the list under <This is a virtual key for removed outputs; DO NOT USE> and deleted it. The compiler had the last word:

e: file:///.../labs/ksp/app/src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/MovingDay.kt:14:31 Unresolved reference 'MovingDayList'.

The third one is the safe retreat. With Dependencies.ALL_FILES, one comment in Lamp.kt made every file dirty, MovingDay.kt and the Java file included: Dirty / All: 100.00%. KSP's own KDoc says it "essentially disables incremental processing". It's correct, and slow.

Notice what all three have in common. A clean build, ./gradlew clean or --rerun on the KSP task, puts them right, because it reprocesses everything. The kctfork tests from lesson 2 pass too, because kctfork deletes its caches and runs a clean build every time. Only an incremental build shows the mistake. The Java side has one safety net here that KSP lacks: when an isolating javac processor gives no originating element, Gradle recompiles every source file, slowly but correctly. KSP believes you.

A generated file that is right after a clean build and wrong after an edit has the wrong Dependencies. Fix them; don't make cleaning a habit.

In the picture, these are helpers who didn't write down which boxes a card came from: the master list goes stale, or gets thrown out with the packing paper. The switch we flipped lives in a file of options, and options have a trap of their own.

try.title: Break the master list, then mend it
steps: Add the line movemate.listDependencies=isolating to labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties and build: ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true. The option changed, so kspDirtySet.log shows every file dirty.

Create Mirror.kt like Rug.kt, with @Inventory data class Mirror(val widthCm: Int). Predict the list, then build with ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true and run the program.
Change the switch to none and build once. Then add a comment to MovingDay.kt and build again. Which file does the compiler complain about?
Mend it: delete the switch line, remove your comment, delete Rug.kt and Mirror.kt, build, and run the program once more.
try.expect: With isolating, only Mirror.kt is dirty (12.50% on our run), the build passes, and the program prints MovingDayList: [Mirror], then fails with IllegalStateException: MovingDayList has no card for Box. With none, only MovingDay.kt is dirty, kspSourceToOutputs.log files the list under the virtual key for removed outputs, and the compile fails with MovingDay.kt:14:31 Unresolved reference 'MovingDayList'. After the mending, the program prints the four names again.

sections.h: Processor options: the job sheet you hand the helper
sections.html:
The master list needs a name, and the processor can't guess it: one family calls it MovingDayList, another PackingList. A processor option is a key and a text value that the build passes to every processor. It's the job sheet the moving company hands the helper, with the address on it. In Gradle you write them in the module's build file:

// build.gradle.kts of a Kotlin module that uses the processor
ksp {
    arg("movemate.listName", "MovingDayList")
    arg("movemate.listPackage", "movemate.lists")
}

// the same options for a javac processor in a Java module
tasks.withType<JavaCompile>().configureEach {
    options.compilerArgs.add("-Amovemate.listName=MovingDayList")
}

In this lab, each lesson's source set has its own job sheet instead, labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties, with lines such as movemate.listName=MovingDayList. The processor gets every option as one Map<String, String>, environment.options, and reads two kinds:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a javac processor's options, passed as -Amovemate.listName=MovingDayList
@SupportedOptions({"movemate.listName", "movemate.listPackage"})
public class MasterListProcessor extends AbstractProcessor {
    ListOptions readListOptions() {
        String listName = processingEnv.getOptions().get("movemate.listName");
        if (listName == null) {
            processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR,
                    "MasterListProcessor needs the processor option movemate.listName, the name of the list it generates. "
                            + "Add -Amovemate.listName=MovingDayList to the compiler arguments.");
            return null;
        }
        return new ListOptions(listName, processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.listPackage", "movemate"));
    }
}
Kotlin
fun readListOptions(options: Map<String, String>, logger: KSPLogger): ListOptions? {
    val listName = options[LIST_NAME]                     // "movemate.listName", null when missing
    if (listName == null) {
        logger.error(
            "MasterListProcessor needs the processor option $LIST_NAME, the name of the list it generates. " +
                "Add ksp { arg(\"$LIST_NAME\", \"MovingDayList\") } to the build file.",
        )
        return null
    }
    if (!listName.matches(Regex("[A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*"))) {
        logger.error("$LIST_NAME must be a class name such as MovingDayList, but it is '$listName'")
        return null
    }
    return ListOptions(listName, options[LIST_PACKAGE] ?: "movemate")   // optional, with a default
}

movemate.listPackage has a sensible default, so a missing value is fine. movemate.listName has none, so a missing value is an error. Lesson 5's rule holds: say what is wrong and how to fix it. An option isn't on any box, though, so there's no symbol to say where, and the words name the place instead: the build file. We deleted the line from ksp.properties and ran KSP:

> Task :ksp:app:kspL07Kotlin FAILED
e: [ksp] MasterListProcessor needs the processor option movemate.listName, the name of the list it generates. Add ksp { arg("movemate.listName", "MovingDayList") } to the build file.
e: [ksp] MovingDay.kt:14: Unresolved reference 'MovingDayList'.

The second line is a follow-on: the list was never written, so the code that uses it can't resolve. Fix the first line. The two sides differ in one more way. javac warns about an -A option that no processor declared in @SupportedOptions. KSP passes every option to every processor without a word.

Now the trap. An option changes the output, so it must be one of the KSP task's inputs, or Gradle skips the task after you change it. In KSP 2.3.14, ksp { arg(key, value) } fills two settings of the KSP task. processorOptions is what the processors read, and it's marked @Internal, so Gradle doesn't compare it. apOptions is an @Input, and Gradle does. Change the value, and KSP runs again, over every file. This lab's ksp.properties fills the same two settings, and the build showed it: we changed movemate.listName to moving-day and ran kspL07Kotlin with no extra flag. It ran, and failed with movemate.listName must be a class name such as MovingDayList, but it is 'moving-day'.

Not every way of passing an option is compared, though. A lambda CommandLineArgumentProvider, arg(CommandLineArgumentProvider { listOf("movemate.listName=$name") }), isn't: in the research behind this lesson, changing the lambda's value left the task UP-TO-DATE, with the old option. A provider class with an @get:Input property is compared. And a provider's values can't contain spaces: Processor arguments not in the format \S+=\S+.

An option that changes the output must be a tracked input of the task. Check it by changing the value and watching the task run.

In the picture, the job sheet goes to every helper the company sends to this house, and to no other house. The picture breaks a little: one sheet serves every processor in the module at once, so name your keys with a prefix, as movemate. does here.

try.title: Run the list without its job sheet
steps: Run MasterListDemo. It compiles two classes in memory twice: once with movemate.listName, once with no options at all.
In labs/ksp/app/src/l07/ksp.properties, change movemate.listName to moving-day. Predict whether ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL07Kotlin runs, then run it.
Change it to PackingList, run the same task, and look in labs/ksp/app/build/generated/ksp/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/. Then put MovingDayList back.

code.title: MasterListDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.ksp.l07.demo import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.KotlinCompilation import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.SourceFile import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.configureKsp import com.tschuchort.compiletesting.kspSourcesDir import java.io.File import java.io.OutputStream import workbench.ksp.l07.MasterListProcessorProvider // Runs the master list processor twice in memory: once with the job sheet (the processor options), once // without it. Uses the reference processor; add -Pmine=l07 for yours. // ./gradlew :ksp:demo -Pmain=workbench.ksp.l07.demo.MasterListDemoKt fun main() { val things = SourceFile.kotlin( "Things.kt", """ package movemate import workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory @Inventory data class Lamp(val name: String, val bulbs: Int, val shade: String?) @Inventory data class Plant(val kind: String, val potLitres: Double, val waterEveryDays: Int = 7) """, ) println("=== with ksp { arg(\"movemate.listName\", \"MovingDayList\") }") val withSheet = compile("with-options", things, mapOf("movemate.listName" to "MovingDayList")) println("exit code: ${withSheet.first.exitCode}") print(withSheet.second.resolve("movemate/MovingDayList.kt").readText()) val list = withSheet.first.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.MovingDayList") val instance = list.getField("INSTANCE").get(null) val lamp = withSheet.first.classLoader.loadClass("movemate.Lamp") .getConstructor(String::class.java, Int::class.java, String::class.java).newInstance("desk lamp", 1, null) println("--- MovingDayList.cardFor(lamp) returns: ${list.getMethod("cardFor", Any::class.java).invoke(instance, lamp)}") println() println("=== with no options at all") val without = compile("without-options", things, emptyMap()) println("exit code: ${without.first.exitCode}") without.first.messages.lines().filter { it.startsWith("e: ") }.forEach(::println) println("generated files: ${without.second.walk().filter { it.isFile }.map { it.name }.toList()}") } private fun compile(name: String, source: SourceFile, options: Map<String, String>) = KotlinCompilation().run { workingDir = File("build/kctfork/demo/l07-$name").apply { deleteRecursively() } sources = listOf(source) inheritClassPath = true jvmTarget = "21" messageOutputStream = OutputStream.nullOutputStream() configureKsp { symbolProcessorProviders += MasterListProcessorProvider() processorOptions += options } compile() to kspSourcesDir.resolve("kotlin") }

try.expect: The demo prints exit code: OK, the generated list for Lamp and Plant and Lamp: name=desk lamp, bulbs=1, shade=null, then exit code: COMPILATION_ERROR, the needs the processor option movemate.listName error and generated files: []. In the app, the task runs, because the option is a tracked input, and fails with e: [ksp] movemate.listName must be a class name such as MovingDayList, but it is 'moving-day', plus follow-on errors for code that uses the list. With PackingList, it succeeds and writes PackingList.kt instead of MovingDayList.kt; putting the old name back may come FROM-CACHE.

compare.title: One master list from many classes: a javac processor and a KSP processor

java.title: MasterListProcessor.java
java.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor @SupportedAnnotationTypes("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") @SupportedOptions({"movemate.listName", "movemate.listPackage"}) public class MasterListProcessor extends AbstractProcessor { private boolean written; @Override public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment roundEnv) { if (written || roundEnv.processingOver()) return false; String listName = processingEnv.getOptions().get("movemate.listName"); // the job sheet String pkg = processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.listPackage", "movemate"); List<Element> classes = new ArrayList<>(roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Inventory.class)); if (listName == null || classes.isEmpty()) return false; try (Writer out = processingEnv.getFiler() .createSourceFile(pkg + "." + listName, classes.toArray(new Element[0])) // every origin .openWriter()) { out.write(listSource(pkg, listName, classes)); } catch (IOException e) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, e.toString()); } written = true; return false; } } // META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors: // workbench.ksp.l07.MasterListProcessor,aggregating

kotlin.title: MasterListProcessor.kt
kotlin.html: class MasterListProcessor( private val codeGenerator: CodeGenerator, private val logger: KSPLogger, private val options: Map<String, String>, ) : SymbolProcessor { override val apiFeatures = buildApiFeatures { enableBackingFields = true; enableContextParameters = true } private var listWritten = false override fun process(resolver: Resolver): List<KSAnnotated> { if (listWritten) return emptyList() val listOptions = readListOptions(options, logger) ?: return emptyList() // the job sheet val classes = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory") .filterIsInstance<KSClassDeclaration>().toList() if (classes.isEmpty()) return emptyList() masterListFile(classes, listOptions) .writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = true, *classes.mapNotNull { it.containingFile } .distinct().toTypedArray())) // every origin listWritten = true return emptyList() } }

compare.note: Both write one file from many classes, once, and both name every class's source as an origin: javac through createSourceFile's originating elements, KSP through Dependencies. The difference is where the category lives. Gradle marks a whole javac processor isolating or aggregating, in a file inside the processor's jar, and falls back to a full recompile when an isolating processor gives no origin. KSP marks each output, so one processor can write isolating cards and an aggregating list, and it trusts what you declare: there's no fallback when it's wrong. Options travel the same way in both, as text keys (-A for javac, ksp { arg(...) } for KSP), but only javac warns about a key no processor declared.

worked.title: A list that's right after a clean build and wrong after an edit: find the cause

steps.say: The report: a teammate added a class with the @Registered annotation, and the generated Registry lost every older entry. ./gradlew clean build fixed it, so the team now cleans before each release. That's the shape of a Dependencies bug: right on a clean build, wrong on an incremental one.
Turn the logs on, add a throwaway annotated file, and build. Then read kspSourceToOutputs.log for the registry's file. If it isn't under the AnyChanges key, the output was declared isolating.
steps.code: ./gradlew :app:compileKotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true # then read app/build/kspCaches/main/logs/kspSourceToOutputs.log: # <AnyChanges is a virtual file; DO NOT USE.>: # (Registry.kt should be listed here)

steps.say: Find where the processor writes the file, and make the output aggregating, with the file of every class it lists. The javac version names every class as an originating element and declares the processor aggregating.
steps.code: // 1. every class on the registry, from this round val registered = resolver.getSymbolsWithAnnotation("movemate.Registered").filterIsInstance<KSClassDeclaration>().toList() // 2. aggregating, from every file registryFile(registered).writeTo( codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = true, *registered.mapNotNull { it.containingFile }.distinct().toTypedArray()), )

alt.html: // 1. every class on the registry, from this round List<Element> registered = new ArrayList<>(roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Registered.class)); // 2. every class is an origin; the processor is aggregating in META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors JavaFileObject file = processingEnv.getFiler() .createSourceFile("movemate.Registry", registered.toArray(new Element[0]));

steps.say: Prove it the way the bug showed up: build, add another annotated file, build again without cleaning, and check that kspDirtySet.log lists every registered file and that the registry names them all. Then stop cleaning before releases.
steps.code: ./gradlew :app:compileKotlin -Pksp.incremental.log=true # after adding one more @Registered class # kspDirtySet.log: Dirty: lists every @Registered file, not just the new one

lab.title: The master list processor: aggregating Dependencies and a job sheet
steps: Read MasterListProcessor.kt. Given: the provider, apiFeatures, the process wrapper, processList with the five moves in order, lesson 2's card written with KotlinPoet (inventoryCardFile), and the teaching switch from section 3. Three functions are yours: one for Check, one for Write, and the Dependencies.

Run the tests: all five fail. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:app:kspL07Kotlin -Pmine=l07. Your processor already runs in the real build and warns w: [ksp] l07 not done yet: read movemate.listName .... Use the KSP task while you work: MovingDay.kt calls the list, so the full compile can't pass before you finish.
1. Find is given: processList asks the resolver for @Inventory once, in round 1.

1. Check: write readListOptions. movemate.listName is required: when it's missing, log the error the third test expects, with no symbol, and return null. When it isn't a class name, log the fourth test's error. movemate.listPackage defaults to movemate.

1. Read and 4. Write: write masterListFile with KotlinPoet: an object named by the option, in the option's package, with a names property and a cardFor function that has one is branch per class, sorted by simple name. The first test shows the exact text.

1. Write, the Dependencies: write listDependencies: aggregating, with the file of every class on the list, each file once. The fifth test checks it from inside a small processor of its own, because kctfork can't run an incremental build.

1. Prove: run the tests until all five pass. Then run ./gradlew :ksp:app:compileL07Kotlin -Pmine=l07 -Pksp.incremental.log=true, add Rug.kt as in section 2's Try-it, build again, and check that kspDirtySet.log and the program's list both name Rug. Delete Rug.kt afterwards.
From memory: close the file and write listDependencies and the two lines that read the options on paper. Then compare.
hints: classes.mapNotNull { it.containingFile }.distinct().toTypedArray() gives each file once; pass the array to Dependencies with the spread operator, *.
For the names, map each class to CodeBlock.of("%S", simpleName) and call joinToCode(). Then initializer("listOf(%L)", names).

For cardFor: beginControlFlow("return when (thing)"), one addStatement("is %T -> thing.%M()", cls.toClassName(), MemberName(pkg, "inventoryCard")) per class, the else branch, then endControlFlow(). %M imports the card when the list lives in another package.
The else branch is a plain string template. %L writes it as it is; %P would choose triple quotes, and the first test compares the whole file.
When the whole-file test fails on one line, open the generated file in the work folder: labs/ksp/build/kctfork/test/<nnn>-writes-one-master-list.../ksp/sources/kotlin/movemate/MovingDayList.kt.
lab.done: All five tests in MasterListProcessorTest pass, and after adding Rug.kt the app's incremental build lists it, in kspDirtySet.log and in the program's output.

drill.title: Write an aggregating output and its options from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A processor writes one Registry.kt that lists every @Registered class. Write its Dependencies, and the lines that read a required option movemate.registryName (with an error that says how to fix it) and an optional movemate.registryPackage (default movemate). Then write the javac version of the same three things. Which of the two languages lets one processor write an isolating output and an aggregating one?

answer.html: val name = environment.options["movemate.registryName"] if (name == null) { logger.error("RegistryProcessor needs the processor option movemate.registryName. " + "Add ksp { arg(\"movemate.registryName\", \"Registry\") } to the build file.") return emptyList() } val pkg = environment.options["movemate.registryPackage"] ?: "movemate" val files = registered.mapNotNull { it.containingFile }.distinct() registryFile(registered, name, pkg) .writeTo(codeGenerator, Dependencies(aggregating = true, *files.toTypedArray())) // KSP: the category belongs to each output, so a card in the same processor can stay isolating

alt.title: RegistryProcessor.java
alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a javac annotation processor String name = processingEnv.getOptions().get("movemate.registryName"); if (name == null) { processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.ERROR, "RegistryProcessor needs the processor option movemate.registryName. " + "Add -Amovemate.registryName=Registry to the compiler arguments."); return false; } String pkg = processingEnv.getOptions().getOrDefault("movemate.registryPackage", "movemate"); processingEnv.getFiler().createSourceFile(pkg + "." + name, registered.toArray(new Element[0])); // Gradle: the category belongs to the whole processor, in // META-INF/gradle/incremental.annotation.processors: movemate.RegistryProcessor,aggregating

recap: An incremental build redoes only what an edit can affect. Gradle skips a whole task when its inputs are unchanged (by contents, not dates); inside its task, KSP hands the processors only the dirty files and restores every other output.

Each output says where it came from in Dependencies. An isolating output, like one card per class, depends only on the files it names. An aggregating output, like one master list, can change with any file, including files not written yet.

An aggregating output hangs off a virtual AnyChanges key, so every edit dirties it, and a dirty output makes every file it came from dirty. That's its price, and the reason not to mark everything aggregating.

Wrong Dependencies are silent until an incremental build: declared isolating, a list shrinks to the new file; with no file, it's deleted. Clean builds and kctfork tests never show it. Dependencies.ALL_FILES is safe and turns incremental processing off.

Options reach a processor as environment.options (javac: getOptions()). A required option needs an error that names it and the line to add, and every option must be a tracked task input, or a new value leaves the old output.

The limit: KSP believes whatever you declare, and nothing checks it. Only an incremental build with ksp.incremental.log=true shows a wrong Dependencies, which is why the next lesson's in-memory tests can't.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our generated list is right after ./gradlew clean, but now and then it's missing classes, so we just clean before every release." Explain to them what's going on, and what you'd change instead.
explain.answer: KSP builds incrementally: it hands the processors only the files that changed, plus the files of any output that has to be redone, and it decides that from the Dependencies each output was written with. A list of every annotated class has to change when a new file appears, which only an aggregating output does. If the list was written as isolating, a new class in a new file makes only that file dirty, so the processor sees one class and writes a list of one. If it was written with no file at all, it can be deleted on a later build. A clean build reprocesses everything, so the list comes out right, and the habit of cleaning hides the bug while making every build slow. I'd write the list with Dependencies(aggregating = true, ...) and the file of every class on it, then prove it: turn on ksp.incremental.log, add a class in a new file, build without cleaning, and check that the dirty set and the list both include every class.

deeper.html:
Dependencies aren't the only thing KSP tracks. Every time a processor resolves a type, KSP records the lookup, and kspLookupGraph.log lists them. On lesson 7's first build it held lines such as src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt -> workbench.ksp.annotations.Inventory and src/l07/kotlin/workbench/ksp/app/l07/Lamp.kt -> workbench.ksp.app.l07.String. The second looks odd until you remember how Kotlin resolves a name: String in Lamp.kt could mean a class called String in Lamp's own package, so a new file in that package could change what the processor saw. KSP's docs call this resolution tracing: a file that resolved a type depends on the files that could change the answer. It's also why resolving types you don't need costs incremental builds, not just time.

A few more switches and facts, from the KSP README and the research behind this lesson. ksp.incremental=false turns incremental processing off and deletes the caches. ksp.incremental.log.graph.origin=<a fully qualified name> writes a kspLookupGraphOrigin.dot graph for one symbol. A file that calls getSealedSubclasses() is dirty on every build, because any file could add a subclass. Since 2.3.14, when nothing at all is dirty, KSP restores the outputs and returns without creating any processor.

Two traps come from Gradle rather than KSP. The labs turn on the build cache, and the KSP task is cacheable: undo an edit, and Gradle may restore the outputs FROM-CACHE without running KSP, so the logs describe an older run. Make a fresh edit, or add --no-build-cache. And processor jars are a classpath input: change the processor itself, and Gradle runs the KSP task again in full, which is why switching between -Pmine=l07 and the reference jar always starts with a 100% dirty set.
